It does not hold for the other `extends` entries, the static parameters, the declaration's own `where` clause, and the `excludes` and `comprises` clauses. The checker lets a member that it checked under the condition be called where the condition fails (ledger row 773).
- A `comprises` clause that lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, as `NatParam comprises { N[\n\] } where [\ nat n \]` or `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`: at a call, the checker gives the variable a fresh size or type, equal only to itself. Two values passed in one call get two. A fresh type is bounded by the binding and by the clause's constraints. The variable is in scope in the trait, except in its `extends` and `excludes` clauses. The checker gives no fresh type where it meets the trait as a supertype of another type. Where the variable is a size, a compiled call that passes a value of such a trait where a listed type is expected fails the JVM's verification (ledger row 307). Departures: a fresh type also under a function type's result (ledger row 751), none for an extender that the clause does not list (ledger row 752), and a crash at a call, from outside the trait, of a member whose type names the variable (ledger row 756).

## The `fortress` commands

`Shell.java` dispatches `bin/fortress <command>`.

- To see what an early phase makes of a program, stop after that phase: `parse` (a syntax check), `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` or `typecheck`.
- `unparse` prints the syntax tree back as Fortress source. Use it to see what a desugaring made.
- `link` links a compiled component (the `link` step of a compiled `.test` file). `api` writes a component's api. `test` runs a program's `test` declarations under walk.
- The command chooses the library. Walk and `test` call `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()`. Every other command calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. Each call points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` to its prelude, and sets the desugaring switches. With `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, `useCompilerLibraries()` points them to the one library (`Shell.java:377-388`).

## Running

    cd ProjectFortress
    # after an ant compileAll that started the caches again: the library order (build-and-caches.md)
    ../bin/fortress compile <path>/P.fss
    ../bin/fortress run P [args]

A small program compiles in about 5 s and runs in about 1 s.

- A crash of the checker prints one line and hides the Java stack. To see the stack, put `-debug stacktrace` before the file: `../bin/fortress compile -debug stacktrace <path>/P.fss`.
- A failed compile of a program leaves a 0-byte jar in `bytecode_cache/`. A run of the program then prints "Could not load P" and "Resource not found". Read the compile's error instead.

## Before an edit

Two notes under `explorations/coordinator/map/` help you find where a fix belongs. A status or a line number in them can be stale. Before you rely on a status, read the ledger rows that it cites. Before you rely on a line number, grep for the method's name.

- Before you add or fix a language feature, print its row of the feature table. WORD names the feature, such as `spawn`, `coercion` or `typecase`. A row is about 1 KB. It names the feature's section of the specification, its parser rule, checker class, walk site, code-generator site, prelude declaration and ledger rows.

      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:spec-to-implementation.md#Feature by feature@WORD'

- If your edit is in one phase, and you need what runs before and after it on each path, print that phase's section. Name the section by its number and the first word of its title. A section is 1 to 3 KB. B.1 is the phase list, B.4 disambiguation, B.5 desugaring, B.6 type checking, B.7 overloading, B.10 the caches, B.11 the runtime and B.12 the natives.

      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:modules-and-phases.md#B.5 Desugaring'

- Before you change the text of a diagnostic, grep the `.test` files for it. A `.test` file can pin a whole diagnostic with `compile_err_equals`, its `file:line:column` included. `grep -l 'TEXT' ProjectFortress/*tests/*.test`, with words of the diagnostic as TEXT, lists the files that pin it. Update each of those in the same commit. A line that you add to or remove from a compiler test program moves the pinned spans below it.

## Testing an edit here

- For a quick loop on an edit of the checker or the code generator, compile the edited class into a scratch directory, and run the compiler with that directory first on its class path. Give each run a fresh copy of the caches, because nothing checks the caches against the compiler that wrote them, and a compile of an unchanged program with a jar writes nothing:

      Q=$PWD/tmp/quick ; export FORTRESS_CACHES=$Q/caches ; CP=$(bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)
      mkdir -p $Q/classes && javac -nowarn -cp "$CP" -d $Q/classes ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/<path>/X.java
      rm -rf $Q/caches && cp -a default_repository/caches $Q/caches
      java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -Dfortress.caches=$Q/caches -cp "$Q/classes:$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell compile P.fss
      bin/fortress run P

  For a Scala file, compile it with `java -cp "$CP" scala.tools.nsc.Main -classpath "$CP" -d $Q/classes -encoding UTF-8 X.scala`. Then put the edit into the tree and build it for real.
- If your change is near transactions, top-level mutable state or the class loader's first load, do the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`).

## The checker's time

This section is for a change of the checker: its Scala under `scala_src/`, or `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` and the generators under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/`, from which the build generates the checker's syntax tree and `Walker`.

The count stage takes `<out-file> <scratch>` and about 80 to 180 seconds, more under load. It can run past the Bash tool's 120-second limit, so run it in the background (`session.md`). It writes a table to the out-file: the errors of each api, the total, the number of places with errors, and the first crash. It keeps the checker's whole output in `<scratch>/run.txt`, and its caches in `<scratch>`, so a run from the base build leaves the base build as it was.

The checker checks every api first, and the component only if no api has an error. In each api or component, it stops at the first of its stages that finds errors. The stages run in this order (`compiler/StaticChecker.java`, `checkCompilationUnit`):

1. The type hierarchy and the type check.
2. The overloading check, which also compares the overloads' return types.
3. In the component only, the export check (`library.md`, "Designing a change").

So the count misses the errors of the later stages, and a fix of an early error can raise it.

The table's rows tell a clean run from a run that the checker did not finish:

- `#total 0` and `#locations 0`: the checker reached the component and found no error.
- `#stopped`, in place of `#total` and `#locations`: the errors came from a phase before the checker, such as the parse. The checker reported none and did not reach the component. The script exits 1, and the gate reads the table as red.
- `#crash`: the first crash of the overloading check that the run survived, or `none`.

If the run printed no error total and was not clean, the script writes no table and exits 1.

The checker's results are the programs that it accepts and refuses, and each error with its text and its place. On the interpreter's library, a change keeps the results the same if both of these hold:

- The two tables are equal: `diff` prints nothing.
- The two `run.txt` files are equal after you replace each run's own tree path with one word, such as `TREE`. Any difference fails.

A node's hash starts from its class name, so an order in the output, such as the apis' checks, does not vary from run to run. A moved order is a difference: keep the old order, or report it.

`Walker`, in the generated `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/nodes/FortressAst.scala`, is split into methods under 8,000 bytes of bytecode. HotSpot does not compile a longer method, and the walker runs on every node. `MethodSizeJUTest` fails if a method of the build grows past the limit, except the methods that its source lists in `listed(...)` entries. Run it alone with `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=MethodSizeJUTest`. If a method of `Walker` fails, lower `WALKER_CASES_PER_METHOD` in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/ScalaAstGenerator.java`. If another method fails, split it under the limit. List it only if nothing in the checker or a compiled run calls it, with its size and what runs it, and name it in your report.

The timing is a smoke test, to catch a slowdown of several times. One run of each tree is enough. A small difference, or one within the noise from run to run, is not a finding. In your report, say what you saw, and do not analyse it.

If you change the checker:

1. Make the change correct, with its tests. Commit it, and name the commit in your report.
2. Time the base build and the change, named `base` and `change`. Run the base in a call set up for the base build (`build-and-caches.md`), and the change in a call set up for your tree, each in the background (`session.md`). Use the same command for both, with `N` the run's name:

       export W=<your tree> N=base ; mkdir -p $W/tmp/count
       time explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh $W/tmp/count/$N.txt $W/tmp/count/$N

3. Make a second pass that makes the checker faster. Start with a profile (below). Where the profile shows a gain, take it. Where it shows none, say so in your report, with the profile's top frames.
4. If the second pass changed code, run the count stage once more with the command of step 2, named `pass`. Show that its results are the same as `change`'s. Then run `ant testQuick` once more (`tests-running.md`, "When to run a whole suite"). If it changed nothing, run neither, and report `change`'s results in place of `pass`'s.
5. If the pass reuses an answer that the checker computed earlier, as a memo does, audit it on one full run. Put the audit in an instrumented copy ("Testing an edit here"), never in the tree. In the audit, compute each reused answer again and compare the two. If any answer differs, the reuse is wrong: fix it or drop it, then repeat step 4. Report the count of reuses and of differences.
6. In your report, give each run's seconds, the diff of the `base` and `change` tables, the comparison of their `run.txt` files, and that `pass` has the same results as `change`.

To find where the time goes, use JFR on the count stage's checker, instrumented copies compiled into a scratch folder ahead of the build on the class path, and the methods over 8,000 bytes that `MethodSizeJUTest` lists in its source. A profiled or instrumented run is neither a timed run nor a run to compare. Print the commands of two earlier speed probes (about 8 KB):

    explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/perf-probes/checker-speed-2/REPORT.md#Decisions, findings' 'doc:explorations/perf-probes/checker-speed/REPORT.md#Decisions, findings'

If your brief asks you to review a change of the checker, run the count stage yourself. Time the base build and the worker's commit of step 1 once each, as step 2 says, with the commit and the worker's head in worktrees seeded at them (`worktrees.md`). Check that your times are the worker's, in order of size. Check that the commit's and the head's results are the same.

content.content:
\section{Overloading Resolution}
\seclabel{resolving-overloading}

\note{
Victor: Does this paragraph, other than the last sentence,
really belong in this section?}

To evaluate a given functional call,
it is necessary to determine which functional declaration
to dispatch to.
To do so,
we consider the declarations that are applicable to that call at run time.
If there is exactly one such declaration,
then the call dispatches to that declaration.
If there is no such declaration,
then the call is \emph{undefined}, which is a static error.
(However, see \secref{applicability-with-coercion}
for how coercion may add to the set of applicable declarations.)
If multiple declarations are applicable to the call at run time,
then we choose an arbitrary declaration among the declarations such that
no other applicable declaration is more specific than them.
A declaration with static parameters is applicable to a call at run time, as
to a static call, when some instance of it whose static arguments satisfy
their bounds is applicable to the call, so the declaration to which a call
dispatches may be one that the static call did not select.
A declaration that the static call selected runs at the instance inferred for
the call (\secref{static-arg-inference}); any other declaration runs at the
instance in which each type parameter is the intersection of the upper bounds
placed on it: its declared bound, \TYP{Any} if it has none
(\secref{type-param}), and the bounds that the dynamic types of the arguments
place on it through the parameter types and that the static type of the call
places on it through the return type.
Where the type parameter is a static argument of a parameterized trait in a
parameter type, as \VAR{X} is in \EXP{t\COLON\TYP{Tag}\llbracket{}X\rrbracket},
the value of the argument fixes it, since no value belongs to two
instantiations of one parameterized trait (\secref{trait-types}); where it is
the whole type of a parameter, the dynamic type of the argument is only a
lower bound, and the type parameter is its bound under the static type of the
call.
The type parameters of a declaration that only dispatch reaches are never
instantiated with \TYP{BottomType}, nor with the union of the types of the
arguments.
\revision{revival-dispatch}{The Working Draft of February 2011 did not say at
which instance a declaration with static parameters runs when dispatch reaches
it and the static call selected another.
The rule stated is the one by which the dispatcher of the type group's paper of
2019 instantiates a declaration (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, ``Polymorphic
Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance'', POPL 2019); the team had assumed
the union of the lower bounds and could not prove it correct.
Both implementations of the revival take the dynamic type of the argument where
the value does not fix the type parameter: the interpreter because it has no
static types, and so no static type of the call to bound the instance, as with
its choice of coercions (\secref{resolving-coercion}); the compiled path because
its dispatcher reads the static arguments of a dispatched declaration from the
value and is not given the static type of the call.
Where the value fixes the type parameter, the two rules give the same instance.
The compiled path's departure is gated as an expected failure (row~538 of the
revival's gap ledger), and the compiled path does not yet run the second
example below (row~496).}



We use the subtype relation to compare parameter types to determine
a more specific declaration.
Formally, a declaration $\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{more specific} than a declaration
$\f(\Qs)$ if $\Ps \strictsubtype \Qs$.  Similarly, a declaration
$\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ is more specific than a declaration $\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$
if $\Ps_0 \strictsubtype \Qs_0$ and $\Ps \strictsubtype \Qs$.
(See \secref{resolving-coercion} for how coercion
changes the definition of ``more specific''.)
Restrictions on the definition of overloaded functionals
(see \chapref{overloaded-declarations})
guarantee that among all applicable declarations,
one is more specific than all the others.
Where declarations have static parameters, they are compared on the parameter
types they declare, each taken over all its instances: a declaration is more
specific than another when the second is applicable to every call to which the
first is applicable, and not the other way round.
Where neither has static parameters, this is the subtype relation above.
No static arguments are inferred for the comparison.
\revision{revival-overloading}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said that
static parameters are inferred as described in \chapref{type-inference} before
the parameter types are compared.
The definition stated is that of the type group's paper of 2011, which checks
it as subtyping of the parameter types read as existential types.}

For example, where \TYP{Shape} comprises the two object types \TYP{Circle}
and \TYP{Square}, of the declarations
%describe[\T extends Shape\](x: T): String = "generic"
%describe(x: Circle): String = "circle"
\begin{Fortress}
\(\VAR{describe}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Shape}\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON \TYP{String} = \hbox{\rm``\STR{generic}''}\)\\
\(\VAR{describe}(x\COLON \TYP{Circle})\COLON \TYP{String} = \hbox{\rm``\STR{circle}''}\)
\end{Fortress}
the second is more specific than the first, although the first has an instance
whose parameter type is \TYP{Circle}.
The calls \EXP{\VAR{describe}(\TYP{Circle})} and \EXP{\VAR{describe}(s)}, where
\VAR{s} has static type \TYP{Shape} and holds \TYP{Circle}, run the second
declaration, and \EXP{\VAR{describe}(\TYP{Square})} runs the first.
And of the declarations
%grab[\X\](t: Tag[\X\]): Marker[\X\] = Marker[\X\]
%grab(a: Any): Any = Red
\begin{Fortress}
\(\VAR{grab}\llbracket{}X\rrbracket(t\COLON \TYP{Tag}\llbracket{}X\rrbracket)\COLON \TYP{Marker}\llbracket{}X\rrbracket = \TYP{Marker}\llbracket{}X\rrbracket\)\\
\(\VAR{grab}(a\COLON \TYP{Any})\COLON \TYP{Any} = \TYP{Red}\)
\end{Fortress}
where \TYP{Marker} is an object with a type parameter and \TYP{Red} an object
type, the call \EXP{\VAR{grab}(a)}, where \VAR{a} has static type \TYP{Any},
selects the second declaration statically; if \VAR{a} holds a value of an
object type that extends \EXP{\TYP{Tag}\llbracket\TYP{Red}\rrbracket}, the
call dispatches to the first, which is applicable to that value and more
specific, at \EXP{X = \TYP{Red}}, which the value fixes, and returns
\EXP{\TYP{Marker}\llbracket\TYP{Red}\rrbracket}.
\revision{revival-dispatch}{The Working Draft of February 2011 forbade both
pairs of declarations, which differ in their static parameters.}

== explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, ## Landed semantics

FACTS.md:271
- F-341 **Walk's numeral is its default, carrying the numeral's four numbers, and converts from them where its place fixes a type.** An integer numeral is a `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ` by its value, a radix-point numeral the `RR64` nearest its value, one value per site (`interpreter/evaluator/values/Numerals.java`). At a typed binding, an assignment, a field, a parameter, a declared return type and a coercion it converts through the place type's coercion from `NaturalNumeral` or `RadixPointNumeral`, run with the four numbers bound as values of type `ZZ`, one result per site and type; a folded constant at a library number type converts from its exact value, outside the coercion; a numeral out of the type's range, one that rounds to an infinity at `RR32` or `RR64`, one at a type with no coercion from it, or one outside its coercion's `where` clause is refused there when it runs; a store keeps its default alone. Dispatch fits it at its default, unless its own coercion reaches a declaration strictly below, which then runs (F-366), else by its own type's coercions only, and reads a tie at the default; a type parameter that several numerals fix takes the narrowest default holding them all. So `q: QQ = 0.1` is 1/10 and `y: RR64 = 0.5` is `SEQV` a computed 0.5, and `h = 0.5` is `true` for `h: QQ = 1/2`, by `QQ`'s `=`, which the numeral reaches by its own coercion, not the library's `=` over `Any` (F-366; `tests/NumeralEqualsNumberWalk`). At load walk refuses a numeral type written as a type that a trait or an object extends, as a type that a trait's `comprises` clause lists, or as a static argument; one written as a return type, a variable's or a field's type loads, and is refused only where a numeral meets it (row 1124). A place whose type names a type parameter calls the method at each evaluation (row 957). A coercion whose body puts two calls of the program's own functions in one operator or one argument list, as `small(n) - small(m)` does, spawns a task, which runs in place inside the root task that initializes the component's class (F-348). Under walk a folded constant at a library type converts from its exact value. Open: coverage refuses a pair when a declaration that it compares has static parameters (row 546). In an accepted family that has any other generic declaration, such a call is typed by its first minimal candidate in the call's order of overloadings, which follows the build (row 935), not by the intersection (row 543). That narrower scope than P-60's is a default. On the compiled path, a method call on a value typed by the intersection runs on the conjunct that has the checker's chosen declaration (F-386), and a generic declaration instantiated at an intersection type dies as it loads (row 559). 9. **Exclusion through a bound, and `tint` (row 786).** Do two parameter types exclude each other when the only static arguments at which they could meet are ones a bound rules out? Walk loads `tint[\T extends Red\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `tint[\T extends Blue\](x: Box[\T\])`, reading two type parameters whose bounds exclude as never one type, and the checker refuses the pair; `Bottom` lies within both bounds and cannot be written, so which path moves is his. The POPL 2019 rules map reads the paper's rules on it, by reading only: [Meet-Excl] goes through existential reduction, which collects the "constraints C that make α different from Bottom" (`Papers/Variance/rules.tex:343-345`), with `unify` and `toBounds` named but given no rules (`rules.tex:252-258`), and no instance is `Bottom` (`rules.tex:159`; `resolve.tex:239-241`, `:773-774`). If `unify` fails on the merged parameter, whose only instance would be `Bottom`, the meet stays unreduced and [Exc-Object-Same] over the two parameters gives exclusion, so the pair is valid; if it returns the merged parameter bounded by both, the pair is refused. The rules state neither, and the Working Draft left the same point open (`Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/future.tex:265`). Its two ways are this item's: the checker's reduction treats an existential whose parameter's bounds meet only at `Bottom` as empty and agrees with walk, or walk's `mayBeEqual` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:1448-1472`) admits `Bottom` as the two parameters' common argument and refuses the pair at load as the checker does; neither alone keeps today's behaviour (`reviews/popl2019-rules-map.md`, question 1).
   - Landed: The checker as it is: yes for a named forced argument, and it cannot conclude it through ancestors (the `CAP` shape); for `tint`, both paths as they are, row 786 `CONTESTED`. The text names the question in Appendix I's "Passages not yet revised".
   - The other way: The text answers it: rung S's "no", which the gather removed, or a "yes"; and walk refuses `tint`, or the checker accepts it.
   - Its cost: A sentence of the overloading chapter, and a walk rung or a checker rung to match it.
   - Home: PLAN, "Climb batch 7b, listed for his review", Whether two parameter types exclude each other when the; `compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/SKEPTIC.md:140` (10-02: 31); PLAN, "Climb batch 19, listed for his review", P.worker.1 and P.skeptic.1; row 786; POSITIONS-history, P-152, its block of 2026-10-22 08:30Z, the former "Left:" list, which named `tint` (row 786); `reviews/popl2019-rules-map.md`, question 1 and sections 11, 16 and 18

323. **P-60's coverage against the POPL 2019 paper's Meet Rule: does the meet of two overloads over closed traits stay covered by several declarations, or does it take one declaration, as [Meet-Third] and the paper's theorem of one most specific declaration ask (P-60)?** The rule: a pair whose domains overlap and do not nest needs a third declaration whose domain is equivalent to their meet, [Meet-Third] (`Papers/Variance/rules.tex:57-61`), so that every call has one most specific declaration statically (`thm:mostspecific`, `rules.tex:509-524`). The decision: P-60 lets several declarations below both cover the meet through `comprises` clauses, so a static call may have several most specific declarations, typed by the intersection of their return types, the declaration that runs unique only at run time (`coordinator/POSITIONS.md:57`); the checker builds it for declarations without static parameters (`coverageRule`, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/OverloadingChecker.scala:676-694`; `coversOverlap`, `scala_src/overloading/OverloadingOracle.scala:188-239`). The type-decisions judgement of 2026-10-23 weighed it: "P-60 is the one step outside the designers' proven model, and it is recorded as such; it stands" (`reviews/type-decisions-review/judgement.md`, V6), and Appendix I says so (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:3514-3525`). #!/bin/bash
# old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...
#
# Runs the old code, the base's: bin/fortress of the batch's one base build, with FORTRESS_HOME set to the
# base build and FORTRESS_CACHES to a private caches folder. If the folder does not exist yet, it is first
# made as a copy of the base build's default_repository/caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). The paths in those caches
# are the base build's own, so nothing is translated, and no worktree is made.
#
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss    the compiled path: compile ...
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P            ... then run
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss            walk
#
# Every cache a run writes goes to the private folder: every cache directory and the logs are under
# fortress.caches (repository/ProjectProperties.java:283-299), which FORTRESS_CACHES sets, and
# bin/fortress_classpath and bin/run_classpath put FORTRESS_CACHES/bytecode_cache on the class path.
# Under the base build a run reads the build, the library sources and default_repository/configuration, and
# writes nothing that stays: the parser writes its error logs beside each file it parses from source and
# deletes them (compiler/Parser.java:349-367), so a compile of a program that exports Executable creates and
# deletes two empty, gitignored logs beside Library/Executable.fsi. Two runs at once may share those two
# names; that is harmless, because the base's library parses without errors, so both logs stay empty and
# a log removed by the other run reads as empty (Parser.java:373-377). Measured in
# explorations/coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md, section 6.
#
# Keep the private folder and your programs outside the base build (the program's own logs go beside it).
# Refuses (exit 2) a base build that is not built, and a private folder inside the base build.
set -euo pipefail
USAGE='usage: old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...'
BASE=$(realpath "${1:?$USAGE}")
PRIV_ARG=${2:?$USAGE}
shift 2
[ -x "$BASE/bin/fortress" ] && [ -e "$BASE/ProjectFortress/build/com/sun/fortress/Shell.class" ] \
  && [ -e "$BASE/default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar" ] \
  || { echo "old-fortress: $BASE is not a built tree" >&2 ; exit 2 ; }
PRIV=$(realpath -m "$PRIV_ARG")
case "$PRIV/" in "$BASE"/*) echo "old-fortress: $PRIV is inside the base build $BASE" >&2 ; exit 2 ;; esac
if [ ! -d "$PRIV" ]; then
    mkdir -p "$(dirname "$PRIV")"
    PART="$PRIV.part.$$"
    cp -a "$BASE/default_repository/caches" "$PART"
    mv -T "$PART" "$PRIV" 2>/dev/null || rm -rf "$PART"     # another run made it first: use that one
fi
FORTRESS_HOME="$BASE" FORTRESS_CACHES="$PRIV" exec "$BASE/bin/fortress" "$@"

export Executable
(* A call whose argument's type sits between two closed traits, one more specific than a third candidate, runs the declaration below them. *)
trait S comprises { U, S2 } end
trait S2 extends S comprises { V } end
trait T comprises { V, W } end
trait U extends S excludes W end
trait M extends { S2, T } comprises { V } end
trait V extends M end
trait W extends T end
object Vo extends V end
object Uo extends U end
object Wo extends W end

f(v: V): ZZ32 = 4
f(s: S2): ZZ32 = 2
f(s: S): ZZ32 = 1
f(t: T): ZZ32 = 3

  assert(f(m), 4, "a value of M is a V, so f(V), the most specific declaration applicable to it, runs; overloading.tex, section \"Overloading Resolution\"")
  s: S = Uo
  assert(f(s), 1, "a U through S")
  t: T = Wo
  assert(f(t), 3, "a W through T")
  println("PASS")
end

end

# Running tests

**track**
: One of the five JVMs of `ant testFast`.

**shard**
: One of the four JVMs of `ant testSystem`. Shard i of n takes every n-th file of the sorted list, from index i.

**code state**
: Code of a tree as one edit leaves it. Only an edit of code makes a new code state; a commit does not.

## The two suites

`ant testFast` runs its tests in five tracks, four at once, in about 11 minutes:

- compiler: `CompilerJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `parser_tests/`. It is the longest track, so it sets the total time.
- library: `LibraryJUTest` over `library_tests/`.
- othercompiler: `OtherCompilerJUTest` over `other_compiler_tests/`.
- misc: the unit `*JUTest` classes, except `OneLibraryJUTest`.
- onelibrary: `OneLibraryJUTest` over `one_library_tests/`, with `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`. It starts when another track ends.

`ant testSystem` runs `SystemJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's test folder. It runs its tests in four shards, in a few minutes.

`ant testSpecData` runs the specification's 130 extracted examples (`SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries`, `advanced`) under walk, in about a minute. The gate runs it after the two suites.

The newest gate summary has the exact counts and times of the last landed run:

    git log -1 --name-only --format= -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt'

The two suites work in the same way:

- Each suite runs `ant compileAll` first, as every `ant` test target does, so it never tests stale classes. After an edit of Java or Scala, that build empties `default_repository/caches` (`build-and-caches.md`, "Building"). Each analyses or compiles the Fortress code that it tests, in private caches.
- Each JVM gets 768 MB, a 32 MB stack and `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, whatever the shell exports. The run steps of the compiled tests get `JAVA_FLAGS=-Xmx4g -Xss64m`, also whatever the shell exports.
- Each suite deletes `ProjectFortress/test-caches` when it starts. Each JVM keeps its caches in a folder of its own under it, so that the JVMs do not overwrite each other's entries. Temporary files go to `ProjectFortress/test-tmp/`.
- The results are in `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/fast-<track>/` and `system-<i>/`, as `TEST-<class>.txt`.

To run a suite:

- Run one suite at a time in a tree, because each suite deletes the `test-caches` that the other uses.
- Read the verdict in the line before `Total time:`: `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` means zero failures, and `BUILD FAILED` means at least one. Every `ant` test target ends with these lines, and exits non-zero when it failed.
- To compare test counts, compare the sum of the four shards. A file added to `tests/` moves every later file to another shard.
- If a suite's count fell, a `.test` file or a `tests=` line almost always went missing.

## The switches that the harness reads

Put a `-D` switch on the `java` line of a run by hand; the `java` line in `harness-one.sh` is a model. On the `ant` line, it does not reach the suites' JVMs.

- `-Dtests=<dir>`: the folder that `SystemJUTest` runs, in place of `tests/`.
- `-Dfortress.suite.shard=i/n`: run shard i of n only.
- `-Dfortress.unittests.count=N`: run N files at most.
- `-Dfortress.unittests.seed=<value>`: the order of the files. Each run prints its seed as `FORTRESS_UNITTESTS_SEED=...`.
- `FORTRESS_JUNIT_VERBOSE=1` for `SystemJUTest`, `-Dfortress.junit.verbose=true` for the compiled tests' classes: show the output of passing tests too.
- `-Dfortress.junit.reset=false`: `CompilerJUTest` and `LibraryJUTest` keep their caches folder. Without it, they empty it when they start.

## Outside the gate

- `ant testNotPassing` runs the interpreter programs of `ProjectFortress/not_passing_yet/`, which are expected to fail. It fails if one of them passes.
- No suite and no stage of the gate runs the team demos, the programs of `ProjectFortress/demos/`. Keep each of the 52 demos that `DemoTests` lists reaching its end (P-79). Check them with the demo driver below, not with `ant testDemos`, whose test of the output is weaker:
  - If your change edits walk, the parser, a phase that both paths run, a class under `nativeHelpers/` that a `builtinPrimitive` string of the interpreter's library names (`interpreter.md`, "Natives") or the interpreter's library, run the driver once, after your last edit of code.
  - Print the driver with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-team-demos/REPORT.md#Commands worked out'`. Save the first script that it prints, under "The demo driver", without the text around it, as `tmp/run-demos.sh` in your tree.
  - From the tree's root, after you set up the call, run `bash tmp/run-demos.sh tmp/demos`. It runs long, so run it in the background with a log (`session.md`, "Long commands"). It runs the demos under walk one at a time and writes `tmp/demos/summary.tsv`.
  - The driver's last line of output, before the log's `EXIT=` line, must read 'demos: 52 run, 52 reached their end'. A demo reaches its end if it exits 0 and its output holds no "fail" in upper or lower case.
  - If your change breaks a demo and you know how to repair the demo, repair it in the commit of your change. Otherwise, report the demo, its output and the ledger row that holds the missing feature, as a defect that your change makes or uncovers.
- Nothing runs these folders: `not_working_compiler_tests/`, `not_working_library_tests/`, `not_working_static_tests/`, `obsolete_interpreter_tests/`, `long_term_not_working/`, `linker_tests/`, `compiler_regressions/`. Put every new test in a gated test folder. A test of a defect that fails today is an `XXX` test there (`tests-writing.md`).

## When to run a whole suite

- The gate runs every suite once, on the tree that lands (`gate.md`). Your brief says whether you run the gate.
- If your edit changes the Java or Scala of the checker, of walk, of a phase that both paths share or of such a class under `nativeHelpers/`, run all the tests that it reaches. Run them once, after your last edit of code. The run needs no commit.
  - For the checker, run `ant testQuick`: the compiler, othercompiler and library tracks at once (below).
  - For walk, run `ant testSystem`. It is the same as its four shards run by hand.
  - For a shared phase (under `compiler/`: name binding, DSL grammars, desugaring, the marking of overloaded calls in `OverloadRewriter`), the parser or such a class, run both.
- Quote the verdict lines and the command in your report, with the commit if your code is committed.
- If the gate later runs on a tree that holds other changes too, that tree is another code state. Your run and the gate's run do not repeat each other.
- After an edit of the code generator (`codegen/`, `OverloadSet`) or the runtime (`runtimeSystem/`), run your own tests, and the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`) if `compiler.md` asks for them. Leave the whole tracks to the gate.
- After every other change, run only your own tests, through the scripts below, and the demos where "Outside the gate" asks for them. Leave the rest to the gate. This includes an edit of either library, though it reaches many tests. After an edit of one of the fourteen components that `OneLibraryComponents.test` compiles, also run `ant testOneLibrary` (`library.md`, "Designing a change").

The suites do not check these:

- the bytecode optimizer, which nothing in the compiler calls;
- DSL grammars, except one program whose phases the misc track runs: `syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss`;
- the linker's aliasing of apis;
- `fortress unparse`;
- the round trip of the `.tfi` and `.tfs` caches;
- a behaviour above one thread that one run of each suite at four threads does not hit.

If your edit is in one of these, your own tests are its only check. Say so in your report.

## One test, or a few

Each script and `fortress junit` below ends with the verdict of JUnit's text runner: `OK (n tests)`, or `FAILURES!!!` with the counts. Read the verdict there: the exit code is 0 whatever the verdict.

### Interpreter tests

Run interpreter tests (`ProjectFortress/tests/`) from the tree's root, after you set up the call:

    explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh <tree>/tmp/h1 \
        ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss [ProjectFortress/tests/X.test] [more files ...]

- It runs `SystemJUTest` with testSystem's JVM settings, at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, on a folder that holds only the files that you name.
- It keeps its cache in the folder `<scratch-dir>.cache`. It starts from that cache while the build and the library sources are those that filled it. Otherwise, or with `COLD_CACHE=1`, it starts empty. Its first line says `cache filled` or `cache empty`.
- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing. After you edit Java, Scala or a parser grammar, run `ant compileAll` first. If your tree has no build, seed it or build it as `worktrees.md` says.
- Give it a scratch directory that holds nothing else. The script deletes the directory when it starts and when it ends.
- If a test has an `X.test` file (its keys for a refusal at load), name it beside its `X.fss`.
- It takes 15 to 25 s with an empty cache, mostly to analyse the library, and about 4 s with a filled one. Name several files in one call to run them in one JVM.
- It shows the output of passing tests too, and removes the Java stack frames.

To see the whole diagnostic, with its Java stack, run the program directly, from `ProjectFortress/` as the harness does, because an import is looked up in the current directory first:

    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress -debug stacktrace tests/X.fss

The direct run and the harness use different heaps (`interpreter.md`, "Running a program").

### Compiled tests

Compiled tests are the `.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`. They link with the library's jars in the tree's `default_repository/caches`. If a build started the caches again, or the tree's caches are empty, run the library order first (`build-and-caches.md`). The tests of `one_library_tests/` compile against the one library, and a run test there needs the jars of its fourteen components. Run the tests in one of these ways:

- `ant testOneLibrary` compiles the fourteen first, with `OneLibraryComponents.test`, in its own caches folder, `ProjectFortress/test-caches/fast-onelibrary`. Each suite deletes that folder when it starts, and only `testFast` and `testOneLibrary` fill it again.
- With `junit.sh`, set `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one ONE_JVM=1`, and name `OneLibraryComponents.test` first. The compiles write to `default_repository/caches-one`, and the jars stay there after the call. Its `FortressLibrary` alone takes about 135 to 160 s, so run the call in the background (`session.md`).
- For a run by hand against the onelibrary track's jars, set `FORTRESS_CACHES=<tree>/ProjectFortress/test-caches/fast-onelibrary` and `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`. The build does not touch that folder, so run `ant testOneLibrary` again after an edit of Java or Scala.

The script is `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`. `climb-batch-N` is the folder's real name, not a placeholder. Run your own tree's copy: it runs the tree that it is in.

    ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh <label> \
        ProjectFortress/compiler_tests X.test Y.test > <tree>/tmp/junit-<label>.txt 2>&1

- `<label>` is any word. It marks the run's lines in the output. The script writes to standard output only, so redirect it to your `tmp/`.
- With `ONE_JVM=1`, the whole list runs in one `fortress junit` run, in one JVM. The compile and link tests run before the run tests, as in the suite. Without `ONE_JVM=1`, each file gets its own JVM.
- It removes the named components' entries from the tree's `default_repository/caches` before the whole list and after it, not between files. So a link test and the run test that uses its jar pass in one call, with or without `ONE_JVM=1`.
- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing, as `harness-one.sh` does.
- It removes the Java stack frames, and cuts each line at 240 characters.
- Its JVMs keep their temporary files in the tree's `tmp/`, and run at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`.

To run the same list in one JVM without the script, and without its removal of cache entries:

    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress junit compiler_tests/X.test compiler_tests/Y.test

Run all the new files of one test folder together, in one JVM, as the suite does. A test that passes alone can fail beside others.

## One unit-test class, or one track

To run one unit-test class: `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=BitsJUTest`. It uses the tree's own caches and the shell's `FORTRESS_THREADS`.

To run tracks of testFast whole, run their target. Each target runs its tracks as testFast does, with the same JVMs and private caches:

- `ant testCompiler`: the compiler and othercompiler tracks.
- `ant testOtherCompiler`: the othercompiler track.
- `ant testLibrary`: the library track.
- `ant testQuick`: the three tracks.
- `ant testOneLibrary`: the onelibrary track.

#!/bin/bash
# junit.sh <label> <dir-of-tests> <Name.test>... : the gather of climb batch N runs each .test through the
# harness in the main tree (fortress junit, the compiled test harness, as climb batch 6.5's gather ran its pair),
# in the order given, so that a link test runs before its XXX run test. Each named component's cache entries are
# removed before the list and after it. First line: the machine line (protocol.md, principle 2).
# ONE_JVM=1 (added 2026-09-29 for the repair on the merged tree, coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md, "A repair
# of tests and records only"): the whole list in one fortress junit run, one JVM, as the gate's track runs them
# together; Shell junit hands the list to FileTests.suiteFromListOfFiles (Shell.java:1086), which puts its
# compile and link tests before its run tests (FileTests.java:997-1004), so a link test still runs first.
# The environment is env.sh's, set here without sourcing it, since env.sh also removes parser directories in
# /tmp. The tree is the one this script is in. FORTRESS_THREADS=4 is the pin of build.xml's fastTrack macro,
# which runs the gate's compiled tracks. The JVMs keep their temporary files, parser directories among them,
# in the tree's tmp/.
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64
export PATH="$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH"
export FORTRESS_HOME="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/../../../.." && pwd)"
unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
export FORTRESS_THREADS=4
mkdir -p "$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp"
export JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp"
FH=$FORTRESS_HOME; L=${1:?label}; D=$(cd "${2:?dir}" && pwd); shift 2
cd "$FH/ProjectFortress"
CP=$(../bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)
echo "# junit.sh $L $(date -u +%FT%TZ); nproc $(nproc); $(grep -m1 'model name' /proc/cpuinfo | cut -d: -f2 | sed 's/^ //'); $(grep -m1 'cpu MHz' /proc/cpuinfo | cut -d: -f2 | sed 's/^ //') MHz; load at start $(cut -d' ' -f1-3 /proc/loadavg); $(java -version 2>&1 | head -1); FORTRESS_THREADS=$FORTRESS_THREADS; tree $(git -C $FH rev-parse --short HEAD)$(git -C $FH diff --quiet HEAD -- ProjectFortress Library || echo ' with the next rung applied, not yet committed'); tests from $D"
clean () { for t in "$@"; do n=$(sed -n 's/^tests=//p' "$D/$t" | head -1); [ -n "$n" ] && find ../default_repository/caches -name "*$n*" -exec rm -rf {} + 2>/dev/null; done; }
clean "$@"
if [ -n "${ONE_JVM:-}" ]; then
  files=(); for t in "$@"; do files+=("$D/$t"); done
  echo "########## [$L] fortress junit, one JVM: $*"
  java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -cp "$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell junit "${files[@]}" 2>&1 | sed "s#$FH/##g" | grep -v '^\s*at ' | cut -c1-240
  echo "exit=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
else
for t in "$@"; do
  echo "########## [$L] fortress junit $t"
  java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -cp "$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell junit "$D/$t" 2>&1 | sed "s#$FH/##g" | grep -v '^\s*at ' | cut -c1-240
  echo "exit=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
done
fi
clean "$@"

component P36NumeralCoercionBodyWalk
export Executable

value object Byte(b: ZZ32)
    coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) where { v < 256 } = Byte(v)
end

value object Digits(count: ZZ32)
    coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) = Digits(n)
end

value object Big(z: ZZ)
    coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) = do
        w = v
        Big(w)
    end
end

run(): () = do
    y: Byte = 200
    assert(y.b, 200, "v converts into ZZ32 at Byte's parameter")
    d: Digits = 00.5
    assert(d.count, 3, "n converts into ZZ32 at Digits' parameter")
    g: Big = 123456789012345678901234567890
    assert(g.z, 123456789012345678901234567890, "v, bound where nothing fixes a type, is an exact ZZ")
    println("PASS")
end

end

content.content:
CP=$("$FH/bin/fortress_classpath" 2>/dev/null | tail -1 | sed 's#:[^:]*/default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache##')
if [ -z "$CP" ] ; then echo "distance: no classpath from bin/fortress_classpath" >&2 ; exit 1 ; fi
MACHINE="nproc=$(nproc); $(grep -m1 'model name' /proc/cpuinfo | sed 's/^[^:]*: *//'); $(grep -m1 'cpu MHz' /proc/cpuinfo | sed 's/^[^:]*: *//') MHz; load at start $(cut -d' ' -f1-3 /proc/loadavg); $(java -version 2>&1 | head -1); FORTRESS_THREADS=${FORTRESS_THREADS:-unset}"

# 1. the shadows, from the tracked sources (perf-probes/prelude/switch-over-distance/make-shadows.sh's
#    steps), and the driver; a text edit that no longer matches is the one way this can go stale
SHADOW="every shadow edit matched the tracked sources"
if ! ( cd "$FH" && python3 "$D/shadow-patch.py" ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress "$SCRATCH/shadow-src" \
                && python3 "$D/add-patch.py" "$SCRATCH/shadow-src" ) > "$SCRATCH/shadows.txt" 2>&1 ; then
    SHADOW="STALE: a shadow edit no longer matches the tracked sources: $(grep -E '^AssertionError' "$SCRATCH/shadows.txt" | tail -1 | tr -s ' ' | cut -c1-200); see $SCRATCH/shadows.txt"
elif ! javac -nowarn -encoding UTF-8 -cp "$CP" -d "$SCRATCH/shadow-classes" \
        "$SCRATCH/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java" \
        "$SCRATCH/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/phases/TypeCheckPhase.java" \
        "$SCRATCH/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/phases/DesugarPhase.java" \
        "$SCRATCH/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/phases/CodeGenerationPhase.java" \
        "$SCRATCH/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java" \
        "$SCRATCH/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/Desugarer.java" \
        "$SCRATCH/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/nodes_util/NodeComparator.java" >> "$SCRATCH/shadows.txt" 2>&1 ; then
    SHADOW="STALE: the shadow sources no longer compile against the tree; see $SCRATCH/shadows.txt"
elif ! javac -nowarn -cp "$CP" -d "$SCRATCH/classes" "$D/DistanceMulti.java" >> "$SCRATCH/shadows.txt" 2>&1 ; then
    SHADOW="STALE: DistanceMulti.java no longer compiles against the tree; see $SCRATCH/shadows.txt"
fi

# 2. the run: one JVM, the fourteen components, FortressLibrary first so that its run checks
#    the apis that it imports, at any depth, with every stage (DistanceMulti.java's header);
#    an api that only a later target imports, as OneShotFlag's, is checked as the tracked
#    method checks it and prints only its count, which table.py reads
RC=
case "$SHADOW" in
  STALE*) : > "$SCRATCH/run.txt" ;;
  *) S=$(date +%s)
     ( cd "$FH" && timeout -k 30 5400 java -Xmx4g -Xss64m -XX:-OmitStackTraceInFastThrow \
           -Djava.io.tmpdir="$SCRATCH/tmp" -Dfortress.caches="$SCRATCH/caches" $FLAGS \
           -cp "$SCRATCH/shadow-classes:$SCRATCH/classes:$CP" DistanceMulti -order check -setting "$SETTING" $COMPONENTS
     ) > "$SCRATCH/run.txt" 2>&1
     RC=$? ; ELAPSED=$(( $(date +%s) - S ))
     rm -rf "$SCRATCH/caches" "$SCRATCH/tmp" ;;
esac

# 3. the table. errors.py's tally and its one-row-per-error list stay in the scratch
#    directory for whoever needs the sites (compare-sites, the review); table.py's rows go

A coercion from a numeral type is generic over the numeral's four numbers, the
static arguments of its type, as
\EXP{\KWD{coerce}\llbracket\KWD{nat} n,\KWD{nat} r,\KWD{nat} v\rrbracket(x\COLON \TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket)},

declares no \EXP{=} with a number type, and no number type declares one with a

Author: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

    A tie that self's type makes in a trait that comprises an object keeps the trait's own declaration, free of the identity-hash order
    
    Climb batch 35's gate repair (row 1100). The checker reads self in a trait whose comprises clause lists types as the trait met with them, and reads the trait's own self parameter the same way, so a call such as denominator(self) in QQ ties QQ's declaration and Ratio's. The tie kept the first candidate in the overloadings' identity-hash order, so the one library's QQ default methods compiled the call at Ratio's arrow in ant's onelibrary JVM and failed verification, which turned the gate red (fast-onelibrary, 40 tests, 9 failures). The tie now keeps the candidates that take self at its trait's type: the call compiles at QQ's arrow and dispatch reaches Ratio's body.

content.content:
(* A generic trait that gives a body to a method which it also inherits with a body, through an extended trait that is not its first, runs its own body, as does a type below it that declares the method again (traits.tex, section "Method Declarations"). *)
component TraitOwnMethodBesideInheritedCompiled
export Executable

trait Eqq[\T extends Eqq[\T\]\]
    eqv(self, other: T): Boolean = true
end
trait Pord[\T extends Pord[\T\]\] extends { Eqq[\T\] }
    lt(self, other: T): Boolean = (cmpx(self, other) = -1)
    cmpx(self, other: T): ZZ32 = if lt(self, other) then -1 elif lt(other, self) then 1 else 0 end
    eqv(self, other: T): Boolean = (cmpx(self, other) = 0)
end
trait Mmx[\T extends Mmx[\T\]\]
    mnmx(self, other: T): (T, T)
    mx(self, other: T): T = do (a, r) = mnmx(self, other); r end
    opr UPPER(self, other: T): String = "Mmx"
    whose(): String = "Mmx"
end
trait Tord[\T extends Tord[\T\]\] extends { Pord[\T\], Mmx[\T\] }
    cmpx(self, other: T): ZZ32 = if lt(self, other) then -1 elif lt(other, self) then 1 else 0 end
    mx(self, other: T): T = if lt(other, self) then self else other end
    mnmx(self, other: T): (T, T) = if lt(other, self) then (other, self) else (self, other) end
    opr UPPER(self, other: T): String = "Tord"
    whose(): String = "Tord"
end
trait Z extends { Tord[\Z\] }
    getter v(): ZZ32
    lt(self, other: Z): Boolean = self.v < other.v
    eqv(self, other: Z): Boolean = self.v = other.v
    cmpx(self, other: Z): ZZ32 = if lt(self, other) then -1 elif lt(other, self) then 1 else 0 end
    e: Late = LateInt(1)
    f: Late = LateInt(2)
    assert(a UPPER b, "Z", "an operator declared in Mmx, Tord and Z, on a Z")
    assert(c UPPER d, "Tord", "an operator declared in Mmx and Tord, on a Y below Tord")
    assert(e UPPER f, "Tord", "an operator declared in Mmx and Tord, on a type whose second trait is Tord")
    assert(a.whose(), "Z", "a dotted method declared in Mmx, Tord and Z, on a Z")
    assert(c.whose(), "Tord", "a dotted method declared in Mmx and Tord, on a Y")
    assert(e.whose(), "Tord", "a dotted method declared in Mmx and Tord, on a type whose second trait is Tord")
    assert(mx(c, d).w, 2, "mx on a Y runs Tord's body")
    assert(mx(f, e).u, 2, "mx on a type whose second trait is Tord")
    assert(cmpx(d, c), 1, "cmpx on a Y")
    assert(e.name(), "Named", "the first trait's method")
    assert(show(Leaf, Leaf), "Marked", "a functional method declared in Shown and Marked, on an object whose second trait is Marked")
    assert(Leaf.sort(), "Marked", "a dotted method declared in Shown and Marked, on an object whose second trait is Marked")
    assert(Leaf.name(), "Named", "the method of the first trait of the object's second trait")
tests=TraitOwnMethodBesideInheritedCompiled

link
run

content.content:
\input{\home/basic/examples/Expr.VarRef.tex}

The special name \KWD{self} is declared as a parameter of a method.
When a dotted method is invoked, its receiver is bound to
the \KWD{self} parameter; the value of \KWD{self} is the receiver.
When a functional method is invoked, the corresponding argument is bound to
the \KWD{self} parameter; the value of \KWD{self} is the argument passed to it.
The type of \KWD{self} is the type of the trait or object being declared by
the innermost enclosing trait or object declaration or object expression.
\marginnote{I thought that for object expressions, the type of \EXP{\mathord{\KWD{self}}}
was the intersection of the traits it lists in its \KWD{extends} clause.
In particular, if it includes a ``method declaration'' with a new name \VAR{m}
(not one inherited from one of its supertypes), we cannot invoke \EXP{\mathord{\KWD{self}}.m},
because \VAR{m} isn't really a new method--just a local function declaration.
(There are other distinctions between the type of an object expression and
the intersection of the traits it extends, so we should think about this issue more carefully.)
}
% The new self-type idiom
If the innermost enclosing such construct is a trait declaration (for a trait called,
say, `\EXP{T}'), and that trait declaration has a \KWD{comprises} clause,
and `\EXP{U_1}', `\EXP{U_2}', ..., `\EXP{U_n}' are the traits mentioned in
the \KWD{comprises} clause, then the type of \KWD{self} is instead
``\EXP{T \cap (U_{\mathrm{1}} \cup U_{\mathrm{2}}
\cup \ldots \cup U_{\mathrm{n}})}''.
If that trait declaration has no \KWD{comprises} clause, or one that lists no type but ``\EXP{\ldots}'',
and has a self-type parameter `\EXP{X}' (\secref{trait-decls}),
a static parameter bounded by the trait itself at its own static parameters,
as in \EXP{\KWD{trait}\;T\llbracket{}X \KWD{extends} T\llbracket{}X\rrbracket\rrbracket},
or by a trait with a self-type parameter that `\EXP{T}' extends at `\EXP{X}',
then the type of \KWD{self} in the bodies of its methods is instead
``\EXP{T \cap X}'';
the \KWD{self} parameter keeps the type `\EXP{T}'
in the signature of each method declaration,
which overloading and the choice of a declaration at a call read,
save the test of whether two overloaded declarations' parameter types
exclude each other, which reads it as ``\EXP{T \cap X}''.
\revision{revival-self-type}{The sentence on a self-type parameter is new.
The Working Draft of February 2011 gave \KWD{self} the type of the trait
in such a declaration,
so that a method body that returns \KWD{self} where the self-type parameter is declared,
as the default bodies of the orders and of \TYP{Integral} in \library\ do,
was not well typed.
The revival reads the self type from the bound,
as the self-type idiom above reads it from a \KWD{comprises} clause,
and checks the declarations that extend the trait against it (\secref{trait-decls}).

### W11. The dispatch method of a generic overloaded function names its component without the package `fortress` (no row)

    Caused by: java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: FortressLibrary
        at fortress.FortressLibrary⚙$seq⟦FZZ32⟧...the_function(Unknown Source)
        at Arr.run(Arr.fss:5)

`OverloadSet` builds the owner of a generic function's instance table and the name of its template class from `Naming.dotToSep(f.tagA.getText())`, the api's bare name, at four places (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/OverloadSet.java:904`, `:1361`, `:1724`, `:1728`), where every other place asks `NamingCzar.javaPackageClassForApi`, which puts a default library's classes in the package `fortress`. The prelude has no generic overloaded function that a program reaches this way; the one library's `seq` is the first. Hack, which is also the repair: the four places call `javaPackageClassForApi`. One small rung with its test, which needs the switch to be seen.

### W12. A carried type has two names at run time, its trait's and its carrier's (no row)

    Caused by: java.lang.ClassCastException: class RangeInternals$CompactFullParScalarRange cannot be cast to class fortress.FortressLibrary$Generator⟦fortress|FortressLibrary%ZZ32⟧
        at ...FortressLibrary⚙$seq⟦FZZ32⟧...the_function

A trait's generated `RTTIc` holds the trait's own interface class (`CodeGen.java:5999`, `cnb.classDesc`), so a static argument read from a value's run-time type is named `fortress/FortressLibrary$ZZ32`, while the descriptors of compiled code name the same type by its carrier, `FZZ32`. The dispatch of the generic `seq` infers `E` from the range's `Generator[\ZZ32\]` and instantiates `Generator⟦FortressLibrary$ZZ32⟧`, which is not the `Generator⟦FZZ32⟧` that the range implements. The prelude has the same two names and never infers a static argument from a carried type's RTTI (its `GeneratorZZ32` is not generic). Hack: the generated `RTTIc` of a carried type holds the carrier class. Part of the carrier design of W2; with W13 and W14 it shows that the design reaches the code generator's naming, not only N5's tables.

# Climb batch 36: the planner's probes

The programs are in `programs/` beside this file: `tests/` for walk, `compiler_tests/` for the compiled path against the prelude. The two patches beside it are the probes' changes to the checker, never in a tree: `tie-log-instrumentation.patch` logs each tie among a call's most specific candidates, and `plain-self-hack.patch` (PROBE 36 HACK, not kept) reads every `self` parameter at its plain trait type in a declaration's signature. Each copy was compiled into a scratch folder and put first on the class path, as the skill's `compiler.md`, "Testing an edit here", gives.

## 1. Under walk, on the base

Through `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh`, plain copies of the expected failures, each prefixed `P36`:

- **Row 1125** (`tests/XXXGenericMethodBoundsDifferWalk.fss` as `P36GenericMethodBoundsDifferWalk.fss`): `FAIL: a ZZ32: 2 =/= a ZZ32: 3; a ZZ32 takes the declaration bounded by ZZ32, the more specific`.
- **Row 1122** (`tests/XXXGenericPairTupleReturnWalk.fss`): refused at load, 'Overloading of ident[\T extends Round\](x:T):(T, FortressLibrary.ZZ32)... and ident[\T extends Shape\](x:T):(T, FortressLibrary.ZZ32)... fails the Return Type Rule: the first is more specific, and i...'.
- **P-174, a numeral coercion's body with no getter** (`programs/tests/P36NumeralCoercionBodyWalk.fss`, new: `Byte(v)` at `where { v < 256 }`, `Digits(n)` for `00.5`, and `w = v` bound where nothing fixes a type): 'Unification error: Closure/Constructor for Byte param 1 ($b:ZZ32) got arg 200:ZZ of type ZZ', at the first coercion. Walk binds each of the four numbers as an `FBigNum` (`interpreter/evaluator/values/Numerals.java`, `convert`, `clenv.putValue(e.getKey(), FBigNum.make(e.getValue()))`).
- **Row 1110** (`XXXExitOutOfTryAtomicWalk.fss`): 'java.lang.RuntimeException: ... exit from nonexistent label block done'.
- **Row 1111** (`XXXThrowOutOfTryAtomicWalk.fss`): 'java.lang.RuntimeException: java.lang.RuntimeException: FortressException: Boom'.
- **Row 1121** (`XXXBooleanOplusNandNorMajorityWalk.fss`): 'Operator OPLUS is not defined.', and the same for `NAND` and `NOR`.
- **Row 1118** (`XXXUndeclaredChainOperatorWalk.fss` with its `.test`): 'Missing expected refusal at load'.

The four runs of the last group: 'Tests run: 4,  Failures: 4'.

## 2. Compiled, against the prelude, on the base

Through `ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh` in the worktree:

- **The checker's choice by hash order** (`programs/compiler_tests/P36GenericTiesDeclaredCompiled.fss`, new): twelve pairs `fK[\T\](x: T): ZZ32 = 0` beside `fK[\U\](x: Box[\U\]): ZZ32 = 1`, each called directly on a `Box[\Blue\]`, the sum asserted 12. In the JVM's default hash mode: 'FAIL:  5 =/= 12; each direct call on a Box runs the declaration on Box, the more specific by its declared parameter types'; a second run, in another JVM, 'FAIL:  6 =/= 12'. Each pair is an independent draw of the overloadings' identity-hash order (row 935), so the test fails on the base unless all twelve draws fall one way, about once in 4,096 runs. Row 1100's own test, `ComprisesSelfAbstractFunctionalMethodCall`, passes on the base in the default mode.

## 2. For the curator

### The words this record uses

- **Walk** is the interpreter. The **compiled path** first checks a program's types with the **checker**, then writes JVM bytecode with the **code generator**, and the **run time** runs it.
- The **prelude** is the small library that the compiled path uses today. The **one library** is the interpreter's library. At the **switch-over**, the compiled path moves onto the one library and the prelude is deleted.
- A **declaration** is one definition of a name. A name with several declarations is **overloaded**, and each call **chooses** one. One declaration is **more specific** than another when the types it accepts lie strictly inside the other's, as a function on `Ratio` is more specific than one on `QQ`.
- A **tie** is a call where the checker finds two declarations and judges neither more specific.
- A **hash order** is the order in which Java lists the members of a set. It depends on numbers that the JVM gives each object, which change from run to run. A choice that follows it is not a property of the program.
- A **trait** is an interface that can hold method bodies. `self` is the object that a method runs on. A trait's **`comprises` clause** lists the only types below it, as the one library's `QQ` lists `Ratio`.
- A **generic** declaration has type parameters, as `f[\T\](x: T)`.
- A **row** is one known defect in the gap ledger. An **expected-failure test** is a test that is known to fail and is marked so; to **promote** it is to make it a plain test once the fix lands.
- A **numeral** is a number as written, such as `200`. A program's own number type takes a numeral through a **coercion** that reads the numeral's four numbers: its digit count, its digits after the point, its radix and its value.
- A **getter** is a method called without parentheses, as `x.asRR64`.
- A **rung** is one fix, built by one worker and checked by a second, the skeptic. A **run** is one launch of the batch workflow. The **gate** is the full test pass before a run lands.
- A **fork** is a choice that the batch makes. Its **default** is the way it builds unless you say otherwise.
- The **checker count** and the **distance** are two counts of the errors that the checker still finds in the one library. Both are 0 today, and the switch-over needs them at 0.
- The **fixed roles** are the agents that every run has besides its rungs: the gather, which merges the rungs' changes into one tree; the review of the merged change; the gate; the commit; and the disk check.
- **microGPT** is the model program. No rung changes a line of it.

## 2. For the curator

### The words this record uses

- **Walk** is the interpreter. The **compiled path** first checks a program's types with the **checker**, then writes JVM bytecode with the **code generator**, and the **run time** runs it.
- The **prelude** is the small library that the compiled path uses today. The **one library** is the interpreter's library. At the **switch-over**, the compiled path moves onto the one library and the prelude is deleted.
- A **declaration** is one definition of a name. A name with several declarations is **overloaded**, and each call **chooses** one. One declaration is **more specific** than another when the types it accepts lie strictly inside the other's, as a function on `Ratio` is more specific than one on `QQ`.
- A **tie** is a call where the checker finds two declarations and judges neither more specific.
- A **hash order** is the order in which Java lists the members of a set. It depends on numbers that the JVM gives each object, which change from run to run. A choice that follows it is not a property of the program.
- A **trait** is an interface that can hold method bodies. `self` is the object that a method runs on. A trait's **`comprises` clause** lists the only types below it, as the one library's `QQ` lists `Ratio`.
- A **generic** declaration has type parameters, as `f[\T\](x: T)`.
- A **row** is one known defect in the gap ledger. An **expected-failure test** is a test that is known to fail and is marked so; to **promote** it is to make it a plain test once the fix lands.
- A **numeral** is a number as written, such as `200`. A program's own number type takes a numeral through a **coercion** that reads the numeral's four numbers: its digit count, its digits after the point, its radix and its value.
- A **getter** is a method called without parentheses, as `x.asRR64`.
- A **rung** is one fix, built by one worker and checked by a second, the skeptic. A **run** is one launch of the batch workflow. The **gate** is the full test pass before a run lands.
- A **fork** is a choice that the batch makes. Its **default** is the way it builds unless you say otherwise.
- The **checker count** and the **distance** are two counts of the errors that the checker still finds in the one library. Both are 0 today, and the switch-over needs them at 0.
- The **fixed roles** are the agents that every run has besides its rungs: the gather, which merges the rungs' changes into one tree; the review of the merged change; the gate; the commit; and the disk check.
- **microGPT** is the model program. No rung changes a line of it.

214	
215	### The words this record uses
216	
217	- **Walk** is the interpreter. The **compiled path** first checks a program's types with the **checker**, then writes JVM bytecode with the **code generator**, and the **run time** runs it.
218	- The **prelude** is the small library that the compiled path uses today. The **one library** is the interpreter's library. At the **switch-over**, the compiled path moves onto the one library and the prelude is deleted.
219	- A **declaration** is one definition of a name. A name with several declarations is **overloaded**, and each call **chooses** one. One declaration is **more specific** than another when the types it accepts lie strictly inside the other's, as a function on `Ratio` is more specific than one on `QQ`.
220	- A **tie** is a call where the checker finds two declarations and judges neither more specific.
221	- A **hash order** is the order in which Java lists the members of a set. It depends on numbers that the JVM gives each object, which change from run to run. A choice that follows it is not a property of the program.
222	- A **trait** is an interface that can hold method bodies. `self` is the object that a method runs on. A trait's **`comprises` clause** lists the only types below it, as the one library's `QQ` lists `Ratio`.
223	- A **generic** declaration has type parameters, as `f[\T\](x: T)`.
224	- A **row** is one known defect in the gap ledger. An **expected-failure test** is a test that is known to fail and is marked so; to **promote** it is to make it a plain test once the fix lands.
225	- A **numeral** is a number as written, such as `200`. A program's own number type takes a numeral through a **coercion** that reads the numeral's four numbers: its digit count, its digits after the point, its radix and its value.
226	- A **getter** is a method called without parentheses, as `x.asRR64`.

(* Under the one library's selection, an exception object without value parameters that a helper raises is that object: IntegerOverflow from ZZ32's sum, FileNotFoundException from opening a missing file. *)
component OneLibraryHelperRaiseSingleton
import FlatString.FlatString
export Executable
overflowIsTheObject(m: ZZ32): Boolean =
  try
    ignore(m + 1)
    false
  catch e
    IntegerOverflow => e SEQV IntegerOverflow
  end
missingIsTheObject(name: String): Boolean =
  try
    typecase name.asFlatString of
      f: FlatString => ignore(makeJavaBufferedReader(f))
      f: String => ()
    end
    false
  catch e
    FileNotFoundException => e SEQV FileNotFoundException
  end
run(): () = do
  println("REACHED")
  largest: ZZ32 = 2147483647
  assert(overflowIsTheObject(largest), "the caught IntegerOverflow is the object IntegerOverflow")
  assert(missingIsTheObject("no such directory/no such file"), "the caught FileNotFoundException is the object FileNotFoundException")
  println("PASS")
end
end

1. **No fork reverses one of your decisions, and by my reading none is consequential.** The ones closest to the line: K1 (`self` keeps its plain trait type in every declaration's signature, `comprises` traits included) builds P-146 on its own stated ground and changes F-225. K5 types row 543's call by the intersection (P-60's text; review-queue item 58's settlement). K8: under the prelude, `c = 0` at `RR32` becomes a static ambiguity instead of a stack overflow (row 528; P-37, nothing added to the prelude). The base build `/home/user/fortress-wsuite` at `4b0e3abd6a` is still usable: clean, idle, and `main`'s code is unchanged since then.
2. **Run 1 (36), four rungs:**
   - **K** (rows 1100, 935, 1112, 1127, 543, and 770 if its test passes): the checker picks a call's declaration by the most specific signature as written, in a stable order. A tie the rules leave is a static error, except P-60's case. The code generator casts `self`, and the gate repair's special case goes.
   - **G** (rows 1125, 1122, 1124): three walk fixes — bounds-only generic pairs, a tuple result, and a numeral type written as a return, variable or field type.
   - **N** (P-174): `Byte(v)`. Each of the four numbers converts where it stands, in walk, the checker and the code generator, and 6 library plus 17 test coercions are rewritten.
   - **C** (rows 994, 1091, 1099): compiled one-library walls, with `Arr` and `Dot` added as run tests.
3. **Run 2 (36b):** F (P-165, the `asRR64` getter), Y (rows 1101 to 1103), B (row 1121), T (rows 1110, 1111). There are two runs because the disk holds four rungs a run, and because N and F rewrite neighbouring lines of `FortressLibrary.fss` (lines 386 to 389), which one gather can't merge.
4. **Probes:** every defect reproduced on the base. The new generic-ties test fails in the JVM's default hash mode (5 of 12 calls right, then 6 of 12). A logging copy of the checker found 66 ties in the one library and 1,598 in the compiled tests; all but 22 (in 15 files) come from the two causes K removes, and those 22 are already settled or already refused. A scratch change reading `self` plain kept the distance at 0 and changed 5 of 1,770 compiled tests.
5. **Dropped or not taken:** none of the planned fixes failed to reproduce. Row 996 is not small (no site traced, and its test compares bytes). Row 1098 waits: item 616 has no default on record, so its rung can't run tonight. Rows 1104 to 1109, 1118, 1123, 1126, 594, 1128 and 1129 don't fit the run size.
6. **Skill:** 14 passages go or change, cited by file and line at `7b7d4c1c56`:
   - run 1: `compiler.md:178`, `:137`, `:49`, `:50`, `:52`; `revival-changes.md:15`, `:99`; `interpreter.md:29`;
   - run 2: `revival-changes.md:112`, `:116`; `library.md:23`; `compiler.md:53`, `:54`, `:156`.
7. **Disk:** 11.19 GiB free now. Four rungs need 10 GiB, five need 11.5 GiB.
8. **Estimate:** run 1 about 5.6M tokens (6.4M with reserve), roughly 5h30. Run 2 about 3.8M (4.4M), roughly 4h. Each landing's review and record-landing come on top (5.78M last time).
9. **Edits I'd want:** PLAN's "Next" and a climb batch 36 line. No new ledger rows and no new queue items. The record-landing list is in the record's section 6, including P-174's two sentences.
10. **Commits, pushed to `main`:** `acb1298b4a` (probes) and `fb9cabb6b5` (the record and its INDEX lines). The record is `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-36.md`; the probe notes are `explorations/compile-ladder/plan-36/probes/fixes-36.md`. Rows 1128 and 1129 from your message are listed as left out for size.
